For liability for non-performance of an obligation (채무불이행), once you show the terms of the contract and the fact that it was not performed as agreed, the debtor can escape liability only by proving there was no intent or negligence on their part (Article 390 of the Civil Act). For liability in tort (불법행위), by contrast, the victim must prove all of the other party's intent or negligence, unlawfulness, the harm, and the causal link between them (Article 750 of the Civil Act).

Suppose a moving company damaged furniture while moving it. If framed as a breach of the transport contract, the company must show it was not at fault; if framed as a tort, the victim must show the company's negligence. This is why, in cases where there is a contractual relationship, non-performance is considered first.
Limitation periods differ

A claim for damages in tort expires 3 years from the date the victim learned of the harm and the wrongdoer, or 10 years from the date of the tort (Article 766 of the Civil Act). A contractual claim is 10 years for an ordinary civil claim and 5 years for a claim arising from a commercial activity. Even if a tort claim is barred after 3 years, there may still be a path if it can be framed as a breach of contract.

Here, the date you learned does not mean the date you first felt the harm, but the date you actually knew that harm had resulted from an unlawful act and who the wrongdoer was. If the calculation is unclear, it is better to go through materials date by date before concluding that it is too late.
Scope of compensation and consolation money

The scope of compensation for non-performance is in principle the damage that ordinarily arises, and damage arising from special circumstances is compensated only if the other party knew or could have known of those circumstances (Article 393 of the Civil Act). This provision also applies to torts (Article 763 of the Civil Act). Mental harm is recognized through consolation money (위자료) where body, liberty or reputation has been harmed (Article 751 of the Civil Act), but in cases involving only a breach of contract, once the financial loss is compensated, consolation money is often hard to obtain.
Comparative negligence also applies to both paths (Articles 396 and 763 of the Civil Act). Either way, if the victim was also at fault, the compensation may be reduced by that proportion.
If both are possible, use them together

If both claims can be made, argue them together in a single lawsuit so that if one is blocked, a decision can still be obtained on the other. Which one to put first depends on whether there is a written contract, what materials show the other party's fault, and how much time has passed. Organizing the date of the incident and whether there is a contract first will speed up the assessment.

If you are the one who received the complaint, look first at which path the other side chose. If the claim is in tort, point out where the plaintiff has failed to prove intent or negligence and causation, and also check whether the limitation period has expired.

author: kang-hyunwoo

title: Money and information to prepare before applying for provisional attachment
summary: Speed matters in provisional attachment, but if identifying the property or arranging security is delayed, the decision is delayed too. This article covers what information to have ready before applying and what to do within 2 weeks after the decision.

body.text: Many people come for an urgent consultation after hearing that the other party has put their home up for sale. Most agree that provisional attachment (가압류) is needed, but when it comes to actually proceeding, time is lost in two places: identifying the property to be frozen, and arranging the security the court orders. Both can be prepared before the consultation.
You can apply only once you decide what to freeze

Provisional attachment is not a procedure for vaguely freezing all of the other party's property; you apply by specifying particular property. For real estate, you check the owner in the certified copy of the register; for deposits, you need to know which banks the other party uses; and for wages, which company they work for. A provisional attachment of deposits in principle affects the balance at the time the decision is served on the bank, so even if you name several banks, nothing is frozen if there is no balance.

items: The other party's name and address, and date of birth if possible
The location of any real estate and a certified copy of the register
The names of banks where they are likely to have deposits
The name and address of their workplace
Money owed to the other party by others, and who owes it (business partners, landlords, etc.)

body.text: Freezing far more property than the amount claimed gives the other party grounds to object or claim damages. It is usual to set an order, for example targeting real estate if there is any, and otherwise deposits or wages.

If you know nothing about the other party's property, you may choose to obtain a judgment first and then find property through a property disclosure (재산명시) and property inquiry (재산조회). Property disclosure can only be used after an enforceable title such as a judgment has become final, so at the provisional attachment stage the court does not find property for you.
Arrange the security in advance

The court may order you to provide security against the damage the other party could suffer from the provisional attachment (Article 280 of the Civil Execution Act). Security is provided by depositing cash or securities, or by submitting a document showing a payment bond contract with a surety insurance company (Article 122 of the Civil Procedure Act). Depending on the property and the case, an order may require part of it in cash.

If you spend several days raising money after receiving the order to provide security, the property may be disposed of in the meantime. If you find out the approximate amount of security at the consultation stage and prepare the funds in advance, you can shorten the time it takes to reach a decision.
Two weeks after the decision, and the main action

A provisional attachment decision cannot be enforced once 2 weeks have passed from the date you were notified of it (Article 292(2) of the Civil Execution Act). For real estate, the court commissions the registration, and for deposits and wages, the decision takes effect only when it is served on the bank or company. Once enforcement is done, file the main lawsuit or a payment order promptly. If the other party applies for an order to file suit and you do not file within the period set by the court, the provisional attachment is cancelled (Article 287).

Even after the provisional attachment, you can still negotiate with the other party. Quite often, the mere fact that their property is frozen prompts the other party to get in touch first, and if an agreement is reached, the usual order is to release the provisional attachment after receiving the money owed.

The deposit or surety insurance you provided as security can be recovered through a procedure to cancel the security if you win the main action. Keep the deposit certificate and insurance policy safe until the case is over.

author: park-jongjin

title: The first week after your bank account or home is provisionally attached
summary: Provisional attachment comes without warning, so it is easy to panic the moment you find out. This article covers what the party subject to provisional attachment should check, the procedures available, and how to claim for losses after the attachment is lifted.

body.text: When withdrawals are blocked in your banking app, or you pull the property register and find a provisional attachment you knew nothing about, that day is usually the first you hear of it. This is because provisional attachment is often decided on the papers without calling in the other side. Rather than calling the creditor in a panic, the first step is to get hold of the decision.
First, check the decision

The decision states who provisionally attached which property, for how much and on what grounds. If it has not yet been served on you, check the file using the case number shown by the bank or on the register and get a copy. The decision also states a release amount (해방금액). By depositing this amount, you can ask for enforcement of the provisional attachment to be stopped or for enforcement already carried out to be cancelled (Articles 282 and 299 of the Civil Execution Act).

Provisional attachment only freezes property; it is not a procedure by which the creditor takes the money. For the creditor to actually be paid, they must win the main action and move on to a final seizure. That also means there are things you can do in the meantime.

If wages or deposits have been provisionally attached, the limits on seizure set by law also apply to provisional attachment. If even the portion needed for living expenses has been frozen, you can dispute that scope, so keep your bank transaction records and pay slips.
Choose how to challenge it

items: If there is no claim or the amount is excessive, an objection to the provisional attachment (Article 283)
If you have already paid or circumstances have changed, an application for cancellation due to changed circumstances (Article 288)
If the creditor does not file the main lawsuit, an application for an order to file suit (Article 287)
If you need to use the account right away, deposit of the release amount

body.text: There is no set deadline for an objection, but filing one does not automatically stop enforcement. If business funds are frozen and the matter is urgent, you can deposit the release amount to release them first and then challenge it through the objection procedure. If the creditor has only made the provisional attachment and keeps putting off the lawsuit, you can apply for an order to file suit so that they must file within a period set by the court.

When you file an objection, the court holds a hearing or an examination in which both sides take part (Article 286(1)). Bring contracts, transfer records and conversation records showing that there is no claim or that the amount has been inflated.
There is still work to do after it is lifted

If the provisional attachment was unjustified, you can claim for the losses it caused. The deposit or surety insurance the creditor provided as security exists precisely to cover such losses. If the creditor applies to cancel the security after the lawsuit ends, the court notifies the party subject to the provisional attachment to exercise their rights within a certain period, and if no damages suit or similar is filed within that period, they are deemed to have consented to cancelling the security (Article 125(3) of the Civil Procedure Act).

If you receive a notice from the court to exercise your rights, don't leave it; check the deadline first. Gathering materials in advance that show losses caused by the provisional attachment, such as lost business, blocked loans or costs spent on the objection procedure, will speed up the assessment. If the losses are not large, it is sometimes better to consent to cancelling the security and close the matter.
Avoid getting angry at the creditor or sending long messages explaining your circumstances because of the provisional attachment. Those messages can be used as evidence that you acknowledge the debt.

author: kang-hyunwoo

title: When a debtor who owes you money files for individual rehabilitation
summary: A creditor who receives a debtor's individual rehabilitation papers has tools such as a trial to examine and determine claims, an objection at the creditors' meeting and an application for an order to exercise avoidance rights. Each has a deadline, so this article goes through them in order.

body.text: Quite a few people who lent money to a business partner or acquaintance come to us for a consultation. They have received a commencement decision and a list of creditors from the court and don't know what to do. Creditors have more tools than you might think, but every one of them comes with a deadline.
If the amount is wrong, act within the objection period

A creditor who objects to the content of the list of individual rehabilitation creditors may apply in writing within the objection period for a trial to examine and determine individual rehabilitation claims (개인회생채권조사확정재판) (Article 604(1) of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act). The objection period is set at between 2 weeks and 2 months from the date of the commencement decision (Article 596(2)1). If you don't apply within this period, the claim is determined as stated in the list, and once entered in the creditor schedule, it has the same effect as a final judgment (Article 603).

If you were already suing the debtor, you don't apply separately; instead, that lawsuit is changed into a suit to examine and determine the claim (Article 604(2)). It is also easy to overlook that the application will be dismissed if you don't pay the costs in advance when applying (paragraph 4 of the same article).
Objections to the repayment plan are made at the meeting

At the creditors' meeting, creditors may state objections to the repayment plan (Article 613). If there is an objection, the court may approve the plan only if the amount repaid to the objecting creditor is at least what they would receive as a distribution in bankruptcy, the debtor puts all of their disposable income toward repayment, and the amount is at least the statutory minimum repayment (Article 614(2)). For an objection to carry weight, you need materials showing hidden income or assets, such as a shop the debtor runs, property moved into a spouse's name, or a vehicle disposed of just before the application.
If assets were siphoned off, an order to exercise avoidance rights

If the debtor transferred property knowing it would harm creditors, or repaid only certain creditors, you can apply to the court for an order requiring the debtor to exercise avoidance rights (부인권) (Article 584(3)). This cannot be exercised once 1 year has passed from the date of the commencement decision, so act quickly once you learn of the circumstances (paragraph 5 of the same article). If the other party has filed for bankruptcy, the bankruptcy trustee investigates the property, so hand your materials to the trustee; if you oppose a discharge, file an objection by showing grounds for refusing discharge within 30 days of the discharge examination date (Article 562).
No direct demands for payment; guarantors are separate

Once the commencement decision is made, compulsory execution or demands for repayment based on claims on the list are prohibited (Article 600(1)). Rather than contacting the debtor out of frustration to demand money, the right approach is to respond through the rehabilitation commissioner, and if after approval repayments do not come in and it is clear the plan cannot be carried out, you can apply for the proceedings to be discontinued (Article 621(1)). If there is a guarantor, you can claim against the guarantor regardless of the debtor's rehabilitation (Article 625(3)).

For corporate creditors, the day you receive a business partner's commencement decision is the day internal deadline management begins. The first task is to put the last day of the objection period and the meeting date stated in the decision on your calendar.

author: kang-hyunwoo

title: With four or fewer employees, can you dismiss as you please?
summary: The restrictions on unfair dismissal and the provisions on applications for remedy do not apply to workplaces with four or fewer regular employees. But if you don't know how employees are counted and which obligations still remain, you can get into trouble.

body.text: Article 11 of the Labor Standards Act applies to workplaces that regularly employ 5 or more workers. So in small shops and early-stage startups, people take it for granted that ‘we have fewer than 5 people, so dismissal is no problem.’ That is half right, because only certain provisions set by Presidential Decree apply to workplaces with 4 or fewer employees. The problem is the other half.
Provisions that drop out and provisions that remain

Workplaces with 4 or fewer employees are not subject to Article 23(1), which prohibits dismissal without just cause, Article 27, which requires the grounds and timing of dismissal to be given in writing, or Article 28, which provides for applications to the Labor Relations Commission for remedy against unfair dismissal (Appended Table 1 of the Enforcement Decree of that Act). So there will be no dispute before the Labor Relations Commission over whether the grounds for dismissal were justified.

That does not mean all obligations disappear. Advance notice of dismissal (Article 26), which requires notice 30 days in advance or payment of at least 30 days' ordinary wages, also applies to workplaces with 4 or fewer employees. Unless a statutory exception applies, such as for workers employed continuously for less than 3 months, you must pay the price for letting someone go without notice. Severance pay also applies to all businesses that employ workers (Article 3 of the Employee Retirement Benefit Security Act), so it must be handled separately for employees who have worked for 1 year or more.

Obligations set by other laws, such as the minimum wage, must also be observed regardless of workplace size. Being a workplace with 4 or fewer employees means that certain provisions of the Labor Standards Act do not apply; it does not mean you are exempt from labor laws as a whole.
How are the ‘four’ counted?

The part most often gotten wrong is counting employees. The number of regular employees is calculated by dividing the total number of workers employed during the 1 month before the date the legal issue, such as a dismissal, arose by the number of operating days in that period (Article 7-2 of the Enforcement Decree). It is not just full-time employees who count; fixed-term workers, part-time workers and casual part-timers are all included, regardless of the form of employment.

Even if the average is below 5, if the days with fewer than 5 workers are less than half of the total when counted day by day, the workplace is treated as having 5 or more. Conversely, even if the average is 5 or more, if the days with fewer than 5 are half or more, it is not treated that way. For a shop that uses several part-timers only on weekends, this calculation can change the conclusion.

items: Attendance records and payroll for the 1 month before the dismissal date
Working days of part-timers and part-time workers
Whether there are family employees and whether they work alongside other employees
Whether another shop run by the same owner is effectively one workplace

body.text: The smaller the company, the more you should keep documents

If the number of employees is near the threshold, the first dispute before the Labor Relations Commission will be over the number of regular employees. If you gave notice of dismissal only verbally thinking you had 4 or fewer, and it is found that you have 5 or more, the dismissal can lose its effect solely for failure to give written notice. Even if you are small, the habit of giving the grounds and timing of dismissal in writing, and getting a resignation letter in the case of a resignation, is what protects the company in the end.

When your headcount is growing, it is time to revise your employment rules and employment contracts together, because the number of provisions that apply increases all at once the moment you exceed 5 employees.

author: park-jongjin

title: Penalties for unpaid wages get heavier from October 8
summary: From October 8, 2026, the statutory penalty for failing to pay severance pay and wages rises to imprisonment for up to 5 years or a fine of up to 50 million won. This article sets out the changes employers should know, from the rule on non-desire for punishment to late-payment interest and treble damages.

body.text: The amended Labor Standards Act passed in April this year takes effect on October 8, 2026. Not many provisions change, but for companies that find it tight to meet payroll, the changes will weigh differently. That is because the statutory penalty for failing to pay what is owed to a departing employee on time is going up.
What changes

When an employee leaves, the employer must pay all money owed, including wages and severance pay, within 14 days, and if there are special circumstances, the date can be extended by agreement between the parties (Article 36). Until now, violating this obligation carried imprisonment for up to 3 years or a fine of up to 30 million won. For violations after October 8, when the amended Act takes effect, Article 107 applies and the penalty becomes heavier: imprisonment for up to 5 years or a fine of up to 50 million won.

Penal provisions in principle follow the law in force at the time of the act, so the previous statutory penalty applies to violations completed before the effective date. However, where non-payment continues past the effective date, which point in time is used as the standard must be examined case by case.

You should also know the procedure. When a former employee files a petition with the labor office, a labor inspector calls in both sides, confirms the amount unpaid and orders payment. If payment is not made by the deadline given, the matter may be turned into a criminal case and referred, and from that point the statutory penalty above becomes a real issue. It is usual to separate the amounts you accept from those you dispute and to pay the accepted portion first.
The rule on non-desire for punishment remains

Some articles say the amendment abolished the rule that a case cannot be prosecuted against the victim's wishes (반의사불벌), but the text shows otherwise. The provision that no indictment can be filed if the affected employee clearly states that they do not want punishment remains after the amendment. However, it does not apply where an employer whose name has been publicly disclosed for unpaid wages fails to pay wages again during the disclosure period.

In the end, a settlement with the employee remains the most realistic means of ending the criminal process in an unpaid wage case. With the statutory penalty going up, a settlement arguably matters even more.
Burdens that have grown beyond criminal punishment

items: Late-payment interest at 20 percent per year from the day after 14 days have passed since the employee left (Article 37, Article 17 of the Enforcement Decree)
Late-payment interest also where regular wages are not paid on the set date during employment (Article 37(1)2)

Where wages were withheld with clear intent, where wages went unpaid for a total of 3 months or more within 1 year, or where the total unpaid amount is 3 months' ordinary wages or more, the employee may ask the court for damages of up to 3 times the amount (Article 43-8)

body.text: Treble damages apply to grounds arising on or after October 23, 2025. The court sets the amount taking into account the period and circumstances of non-payment, how much effort the employer made to pay, late-payment interest already paid and the employer's financial situation. If non-payment is unavoidable, drawing up a payment plan and keeping a record of paying at least part of it first will matter in this assessment.

If cash flow makes it difficult to pay severance, start by signing an extension agreement with the employee before the 14 days are up. A single agreement stating the date and amount can make a big difference to late-payment interest and criminal liability.

author: park-jongjin

title: A response to an unfair dismissal remedy application starts from the dismissal notice
summary: When the Labor Relations Commission sends a copy of a remedy application, the company must prove that the dismissal was justified. This article sets out the order in which to prepare the response and the hearing.

body.text: A common trap companies fall into in Labor Relations Commission cases is thinking that because the employee did something wrong, the dismissal is naturally justified. When a dismissed employee applies for remedy, the company receives a copy of the application and a request to submit a response, and company heads usually have a lot to say: how long they put up with it, and how the other employees all knew. But the Labor Relations Commission looks at whether that story can be turned into a record.
Three things the company must prove

Whether the grounds for dismissal actually existed, whether those grounds were serious enough to justify dismissal, and whether the required procedures were followed. The company bears the burden of proving just cause for dismissal. The fact that you warned the employee verbally several times is hard to have recognized unless it is preserved in a warning letter or email.

A dismissal takes effect only if its grounds and timing are given in writing (Article 27 of the Labor Standards Act). The response should be written around the grounds stated in the notice. Bringing up new grounds in the response that were not in the notice weakens its persuasiveness, and if the grounds in the notice are too abstract, that itself may be pointed out as a procedural problem.
What to do in the week you receive the copy

items: Put the deadline for the response set by the Labor Relations Commission on the calendar
Check the original dismissal notice and how it was sent (mail, email, messenger)
Gather the notice of the disciplinary committee, its minutes and records of giving the employee a chance to explain
Break down the employee's claims item by item and mark which ones you have rebuttal materials for and which you don't

body.text: Doing this marking exercise reveals the company's weak points. If the grounds are clear but you skipped the notice convening the disciplinary committee required by the employment rules, the dismissal may be found unfair even if the grounds are sufficient. You need to know your weak points first to decide whether to settle or fight to the end.

In the response, set out in order the background of the case, the facts and evidence for each ground of dismissal, why the disciplinary measure was proportionate, and how the procedures were followed. If you rebut the parts of the employee's claims that are untrue using matching item numbers, it is easier for the commissioners to read both sides' arguments side by side.

If there are 4 or fewer regular employees, the provisions restricting dismissal and on remedy applications do not apply. However, the number of regular employees is calculated by dividing the total number of workers over a set period by the number of operating days, so recount including part-timers.
The hearing and settlement

After the investigator's fact-finding, a hearing is held at which the commissioners question both sides directly. It is a good idea to practice in advance with expected questions so that the answers of the company head or HR manager do not contradict the response. If you number the evidence submitted with the response and indicate in the text which argument each item supports, you can find and point to it immediately at the hearing too.

The Labor Relations Commission may recommend a settlement before issuing its decision, and a settlement reached has the same effect as a judicial settlement (Article 16-3 of the Labor Relations Commission Act). If there are flaws in the procedure, it is worth comparing a monetary settlement rather than waiting for the decision. This is because if a remedy order is not complied with after a finding of unfair dismissal, a non-compliance penalty of up to 30 million won can be imposed repeatedly, up to twice a year (Article 33 of the Labor Standards Act).

If you disagree with the decision, you can apply to the National Labor Relations Commission for review within 10 days of being notified of the written decision (Article 31). The deadline is short, so be sure to note the date you received the decision.

author: kang-hyunwoo

title: Penalty clauses: look at their nature before the numbers
summary: A penalty in a contract may be liquidated damages, which a court can reduce, or a contractual penalty, which it may not. This article explains why you should settle which one it is in the wording before signing.

body.text: The first thing companies ask when they bring us a contract to review is usually the amount: isn't a penalty of twice the contract price too much, or conversely, isn't the penalty we would receive too small? But there is something to look at before the amount: what legal nature that money has.
A penalty is presumed to be liquidated damages

Article 398(4) of the Civil Act presumes that an agreement on a penalty is a predetermination of damages (손해배상액의 예정), i.e. liquidated damages. Liquidated damages are a device that allows you to claim the agreed amount when a dispute arises without proving how much the actual loss was. This is convenient for the receiving side, but it comes with a limitation: even if the actual loss exceeds the predetermined amount, it is in principle hard to receive more than that.

If the predetermined amount is unreasonably high, the court may reduce it appropriately (paragraph 2 of the same article). So for the paying side, the amount written in the contract is not the end of the story. There remains room to seek a reduction based on the size of the transaction, how the breach happened and the loss that could actually arise.

Having liquidated damages also does not take away the right to demand performance or to rescind the contract (paragraph 3 of the same article). You can choose separately whether to end the deal while receiving the penalty or to keep demanding performance. Delay penalties (지체상금) charged per day when delivery or construction runs late raise the same issue. Without a cap, they can exceed the contract price as the delay drags on, and then too, whether to reduce them becomes an issue.
What changes if you write ‘contractual penalty’

If the contract clearly states that the penalty is a contractual penalty (위약벌), things may be different. A contractual penalty is money received as a sanction for breach, so it is generally considered claimable separately from damages, and the reduction provision in Article 398(2) may not apply as is. However, an excessively heavy contractual penalty may be partly void as contrary to public order.

Even with the same figure, the size of the company's liability differs depending on whether it is liquidated damages or a contractual penalty, and whether actual losses can be claimed separately. If this is left blank, any dispute will start with an argument over interpretation.
Is your company the receiving side or the paying side?

If you are more likely to receive the penalty, consider adding a sentence that actual losses can be claimed separately from the penalty, or stating that it is a contractual penalty. If you are more likely to pay, specify that the penalty is liquidated damages and include an overall liability cap and an exclusion of indirect damages.

When reviewing, check in turn whether the nature of the penalty is settled in the wording, whether actual losses can be claimed separately from the penalty, whether there is an overall liability cap and an exclusion of indirect damages, and whether a cure period is given to correct a breach.
Even if the other side has used the form dozens of times, these few lines are worth negotiating. Once you have signed, there is not much you can do other than hope for a reduction by the court.

author: park-jongjin

title: Asking a business partner to revise a contract: there is an order to it
summary: Many people worry that asking for revisions will break the deal. This article explains how to sort out what to fix first rather than holding on to every clause.

body.text: “If we ask for this many changes, won't the other company be unhappy?” That is what clients add most often when they bring us a contract to review. The side that receives the other party's form always feels like the weaker party. But when deals actually fall through, the problem was often not the request for revisions itself but the way it was made.
Sort clauses into three columns

When you receive a contract, sort the clauses into those you must fix, those worth negotiating and those you can accept. Clauses with no cap on damages or that require compensation for ‘all losses’, clauses that let only the other side terminate, and clauses with vague payment timing usually go in the first column. Clauses such as the competent court or the method of notice often go in the second.

The trick is to narrow the first column down to no more than two or three. If you send back a contract with red lines in twenty places, the other side's contact person will pass it straight to their legal team, and from then on the schedule gets longer.

If it is a form the other side uses unchanged with many business partners, it may be regarded as standard terms and conditions. The Act on the Regulation of Terms and Conditions treats contract terms prepared in advance for contracting with multiple parties as standard terms regardless of their name or form (Article 2 of that Act), and makes unfair clauses void. Some companies carefully add this point as grounds for their revision request.
Send the revised wording together with the reason

If you only send “This clause is a problem,” the other side won't know what to accept. Instead, write the replacement sentence yourself and add a line or two on why it is needed, and you will get a faster reply. For example, if you propose capping damages at the contract price while excepting intent or gross negligence, the other side also has a reason to accept it.

Look at penalties in terms of numbers. A penalty is presumed to be liquidated damages and can be reduced by the court if excessive (Article 398 of the Civil Act), but things may be different if the contract describes it as a contractual penalty (위약벌). The direction of the revision is also reversed depending on whether your company is the paying side or the receiving side.

Reading only the main text and skipping the attachments is another common mistake. If a specification or quotation says something different from the main text, you need to settle which one prevails, and also check whether delivery dates or unit prices agreed verbally in meetings made it into the final version.
If some clauses could not be changed in the end

Some clauses cannot be changed even through negotiation. In that case, set out by email how you understand the clause as you sign, and send it to the other side once. Record in the same way anything the other side's contact person said verbally, such as “we don't actually use that clause.”
If a dispute arises later, records like these are what gets looked at after the contract. A few emails exchanged in the days before signing can protect the company's position years later.

Finally, check the authority of the person signing. If someone other than the CEO is signing for the other side, check whether that person has authority to contract on the company's behalf, and whether the deal requires board approval within your own company.

author: park-jongjin

title: The limitation period for payment for goods may be 3 years, not 5
summary: Companies that remember only the 5-year limitation period for commercial claims sometimes miss a short 3-year period. This article looks at limitation periods by type of receivable and how to stop the clock.

body.text: When talking about a company's receivables, you often hear that ‘commercial claims last 5 years.’ That is not wrong. Article 64 of the Commercial Act sets the extinctive prescription period for claims arising from commercial activities at 5 years. The problem is the proviso in the same article: if another law provides a shorter period, that provision applies.
The 3-year periods in the Civil Act

Article 163 of the Civil Act lists claims that expire after 3 years. Even picking out only the items relevant to company practice, there are quite a few: payment for products and goods sold by producers and merchants, claims relating to the work of craftsmen and manufacturers, claims of a contractor relating to construction work, and fees and interest set for periods of 1 year or less.

So a manufacturer's payment for delivered goods or a wholesaler's or retailer's payment for goods sold on credit may need to be acted on within 3 years. Equipment rental fees payable monthly may also be subject to the short period. Which category applies has to be determined by looking at the transaction, so lumping everything together as a single line of ‘receivables’ in your books is risky.

items: Payment for goods sold by a merchant and claims relating to a manufacturer's work: 3 years
A contractor's claim for construction payments: also 3 years
Other claims from commercial activities: 5 years in principle
Claims confirmed by a judgment or mediation: 10 years (Article 165 of the Civil Act)

body.text: The limitation period runs from when payment can be claimed. If a payment date was set, it runs from that date; if not, in principle from the time of delivery. For transactions with deliveries in several installments, the period can run separately for each one, so if you relax by looking only at the date of the last transaction, the oldest payments may expire first.
A certified letter alone does not stop the clock

The limitation period is interrupted by a claim, by seizure, provisional attachment or provisional injunction, or by the debtor's acknowledgment (Article 168 of the Civil Act). What is often misunderstood here is the certified letter (내용증명). Demanding payment by certified letter is only an out-of-court demand (최고), and such a demand does not interrupt the limitation period unless you take a step such as a lawsuit or provisional attachment within 6 months (Article 174 of the Civil Act).

If the limitation period has only a few months left, think of the 6 months from the date you send the certified letter not as a deadline but as a starting point. Conversely, if the business partner stamped a balance confirmation or acknowledged the remaining debt while paying part of it, the period may start running anew because of that acknowledgment, so keep such documents together separately.

The longer you have dealt with a partner, the more you tend to put off demanding payment. If you establish a practice of exchanging receivable balance confirmations every quarter, you can manage limitation periods without harming the relationship. If you have claims that are already close to 3 years old, we recommend considering a payment order or provisional attachment first, even if the amounts are not large.

Provisional attachment both stops the limitation period and freezes the other party's property. If you hear rumors that a business partner's situation is deteriorating, that is one more reason to move quickly, regardless of the limitation period.

author: park-jongjin

title: Why ‘I only passed on the money’ does not work as a defense
summary: Couriers who collect and hand over cash are investigated as accomplices in voice phishing fraud. We look at how courts assess intent, and at the new reduction provision introduced in September 2026.

body.text: High daily pay, a job delivering documents, interviews held over a messenger app. Open the file in a voice phishing courier case and the story usually begins with a job ad like this. People facing questioning say the same thing every time: “I just did what I was told and passed on the money.” Even if that is true, it is not enough on its own to clear the charge.
Intent can be found even if you did not know for sure

Even if you did not clearly know it was voice phishing, courts find intent if you thought it might be illegal and carried on with the work anyway. This is what is called dolus eventualis (미필적 고의). So rather than repeating that you did not know, it matters far more to show, with records, why you believed at the time that it was a legitimate job.

Small actions, such as whether you searched the company name when you were hired, checked its business registration, or how you explained the new job to family or friends, can serve as circumstances showing you believed the job was legitimate. On the other hand, the circumstances investigators ask about are almost always the same.

items: Whether you were hired only through a messenger app, with no employment contract or face-to-face interview
Whether the pay was excessive for the work involved
Whether you were told to pretend to be someone else or to delete chat rooms
Whether you split the cash you received into several cash deposits made without a bankbook

body.text: Going out even once does not end lightly

A person who collected and passed on money is investigated as a co-principal or an aider and abettor in fraud. Following an amendment on December 23, 2025, the statutory penalty for fraud is now imprisonment of up to 20 years or a fine of up to 50 million won, and Article 15-2 of the Special Act on the Prevention of Damage from Telecommunications Financial Fraud and Refund of Damaged Assets (전기통신금융사기 피해 방지 및 피해자산 환급에 관한 특별법) provides for imprisonment for a definite term of at least one year or a fine of three to five times the criminal proceeds.

If the scope of the conspiracy is read broadly, losses you never collected yourself can end up in the charges. The starting point of the defense is to pin down precisely from when to when, how many times, and from whom you collected money.

If your mobile phone has been seized, you can apply to take part in the forensic process and watch what data is extracted. It is a chance to check whether only data unfavorable to you is being picked out, and whether conversations showing that you were used have been left out.

Because couriers meet victims in person, they are the first to be identified, and if they went out several times or the amounts are large, an arrest may be followed by a request for a detention warrant. Restoring the victims' losses weighs heavily in sentencing, so where there are several victims we try to reach a settlement with each one, and for victims who cannot be reached we consider a criminal deposit (형사공탁).
The new reduction provision

On September 8, 2026, Article 17-2 was added to the same Act. It provides that the sentence may be reduced or waived for a person who, during the investigation or trial, gives statements or materials revealing other people's crimes, or provides information about catching offenders or about criminal proceeds. It also applies to cases under investigation or on trial when it took effect.

With this provision in mind, deleting Telegram chats or resetting your phone out of fear hurts you twice over. You come under suspicion of trying to destroy evidence, and you also throw away the very material that could expose the organization. Leave the instruction messages, the screens of the job ad and the records of the pay you received as they are, and we recommend deciding what to submit, and when, before you are questioned.

author: kim-hansol

title: If you only sent your debit card and received no money
summary: Many people are investigated under the Electronic Financial Transactions Act after handing over a debit card and PIN to get a loan. We look at the difference between transfer and lending, and what counts as consideration.

body.text: A message saying you need to build up a transaction history to get a loan limit, so please send your debit card and PIN. Quite a few people believe this, send the card by courier, and a few weeks later get a call from the police station. Most of them say, “I didn't receive a single won.” But what matters in these cases is not money received but something you were promised in return.
What the law targets is the means of access, not the bank account

People usually say they ‘lent their bankbook’, but what the Electronic Financial Transactions Act (전자금융거래법) punishes is dealing in means of access (접근매체). These include the tools and information used to move money out of an account, such as debit cards, cash cards, certificates and passwords. Even if you handed over no physical item and only shared information, it may still apply if you allowed someone else to transact through your account.
A violation is punishable by imprisonment of up to five years or a fine of up to 30 million won, and both may be imposed together (Article 49(4) and (8) of the Electronic Financial Transactions Act).
Transfer and lending have different requirements

Transferring an account outright is punishable even without consideration. Lending it for someone to use for a period, on the other hand, is punishable when consideration is given, received or promised, or when you knew it would be used for crime. So in lending cases, what the other party offered to do for you when you sent the card decides the outcome.

In a case where a person who would normally have had difficulty getting a loan sent a debit card in exchange for the chance to build a transaction record and obtain a loan, the Supreme Court held that the chance itself could be consideration for the lending (Supreme Court Decision 2017Do16946, June 27, 2019). This is why saying you received no money does not lead straight to a finding of no charge.

Of course, not every case ends in a conviction. The judgment can differ depending on how convincingly the other party impersonated a financial company, whether you were to get the card back, and whether you reported it immediately once you felt something was wrong.

If voice phishing proceeds came into the account you handed over, you may be investigated not only for violating the Electronic Financial Transactions Act but also for aiding fraud or as an accomplice. If you withdrew that money yourself or sent it to another account as instructed, the charges become much more serious.

What about lending your card to a family member for a short while? If you let them use it briefly with no consideration and did not know it would be used for crime, lending in itself is not punished. But if you handed it over outright, that is a transfer even without consideration, and if the card is used for crime, the account holder will also find it hard to avoid investigation.
Inconveniences that remain even if it ends with a fine

In a case related to voice phishing, you may be designated as a person restricted from electronic financial transactions for three years even if you only receive a fine, and for five years if you receive a prison sentence, including a suspended one. Once internet banking is blocked, even salary transfers and paying utility bills become inconvenient. That is why you need to take this consequence into account when responding at the disposition stage.

If you receive notice that your account has been suspended from payment, first check the deadline for filing an objection, and keep the texts and call records you exchanged with the other party rather than deleting them. An objection to a payment suspension is not accepted if the account holder appears to have known, or through gross negligence failed to know, that the account was being used for fraud, so the records explaining the situation when you sent the card are used here as well.

author: kim-hansol

title: I only asked for a blood test, so why is it refusal of a breath test?
summary: Refusing a sobriety test carries a heavier statutory penalty than drunk driving below 0.2 percent. We look at the Supreme Court's standard for refusal, the order of breath testing and blood sampling, and what refusing a screening device means.

body.text: At checkpoints, some drivers say, “I don't trust the breath test, so take my blood instead.” It was only a request to be measured accurately, made out of a sense of injustice, but by the time they are questioned the charge has become refusal of a sobriety test. This one matter of order makes a bigger difference than you might think.
Why refusal is punished more heavily

A driver who fails to comply with a sobriety test when there are reasonable grounds to believe they are under the influence of alcohol is punishable by imprisonment of one to five years or a fine of 5 million to 20 million won (Article 148-2(2) of the Road Traffic Act). This applies regardless of the actual reading, so you may be punished more heavily than if you had been measured below 0.2 percent. Obstructing a sobriety test, by drinking more after driving in order to make measurement difficult, is punished with the same penalty.

The same goes for your license. If you refuse a test, your license is always revoked, and you are excluded from the reduction available for people who drive to earn a living. The disqualification period is one year in principle, but two years if you caused an accident or if drunk driving and test refusal together add up to two or more times (Article 82(2) of the Road Traffic Act).
A blood test is the step after a breath test

The Road Traffic Act provides that measurement is first made by breath test, and that a driver who disputes the result may be measured again by blood sample with their consent (Article 44(2) and (3)). A blood test is a procedure for disputing the result, so if you skip the breath test altogether and insist on a blood test from the start, there is a risk it will be treated as refusal. However unfair it feels, the proper order is to take the breath test first, state clearly that you do not accept the result, and then ask for a blood test.
Failing to blow properly a few times is not automatically refusal

The Supreme Court regards a failure to comply with a test as a case where it is objectively clear that the driver has no intention of complying. It decides this by looking at the driver's words and conduct at the time, how and in what way the officer requested the test, documents such as the detection report, and the reasons for and length of the refusal as a whole (Supreme Court Decision 2016Do16121, June 8, 2017).

The same decision held that refusing the earlier screening step with an alcohol detector, while knowing that a breathalyzer test was to follow, can also amount to refusal. Do not assume it is fine because the detector is not the formal test. On the other hand, if you were not driving, or if the alcohol was drunk elsewhere well after you had finished driving, you can challenge the very basis for demanding the test.

If lung disease or an injury made it hard to blow enough air, you need to show this with a medical certificate and treatment records. Write down in chronological order how many times you tried, whether the officer explained how to do it, and what was said between each attempt.
Be even more careful if there was an accident

If you cause an accident injuring someone and do not comply with a test request, you can be prosecuted even if you have comprehensive insurance or the victim does not want you punished (Article 3(2) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents (교통사고처리 특례법)). Cases where the driver requested or agreed to a blood test are excluded from this exception, so at an accident scene what was said during the testing process is especially important.

author: kim-hansol

title: I wrote the truth, so why is it defamation?
summary: It can be defamation even if you did not lie. We go through, in order, the punishment of stating true facts, public interest purpose, the possibility of spreading, and the 2026 amendment to the Network Act.

body.text: “Everything I wrote is true.” This is the first thing people accused of defamation say in the consultation room. It is said with a sense of injustice, but unfortunately that fact alone does not end the case. Korean criminal law punishes the disclosure of true facts as well.
The provision that punishes even the truth

Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act provides that a person who defames another by publicly stating facts is punishable by imprisonment with or without labor for up to two years or a fine of up to 5 million won. There has been debate over whether this provision restricts freedom of expression too much, but the Constitutional Court held it constitutional (Constitutional Court Decision 2017HunMa1113 and others, February 25, 2021).

There is, however, one way out. If the facts are true and solely in the public interest, the act is not punished (Article 310 of the Criminal Act). Reviews written to inform other consumers, and warning posts meant to prevent the same harm, are argued mainly on this point. Whether you wrote only verifiable facts, such as dates, amounts and what was said, and whether personal attacks were mixed in, weigh heavily in the judgment.
When words said to one person can spread

Defamation requires publicity (공연성). The Supreme Court maintains the position that even if you spoke to only one or two people, publicity can be found if they might pass it on to others (Supreme Court en banc Decision 2020Do5813, November 19, 2020). Conversely, if you spoke only to family or to someone in a relationship of confidentiality, the possibility of spreading may be denied.

Another common defense is that you did not use the person's name. Even if you used only initials or a nickname, the victim is treated as identified if people around them can tell who it is by putting together the company name, job title, neighborhood or photos.
For online posts, the issue is intent to slander

Posts on blogs, online communities, social media and review boards are often investigated under Article 70 of the Network Act (정보통신망법). If the facts are true, the penalty is imprisonment of up to three years or a fine of up to 30 million won; if false, imprisonment of up to seven years, suspension of qualifications for up to ten years, or a fine of up to 70 million won. The 70 million won cap on fines for false facts applies to acts committed after the amended provision took effect on January 6, 2026, and the previous standard applies to earlier acts.

This provision punishes only where there is intent to slander. If the main motive for a post was the public interest, the judgment may lean toward denying intent to slander, so why you wrote the post becomes the center of the case.

Under both the Criminal Act and the Network Act, defamation is an offense that cannot be prosecuted against the victim's wishes (반의사불벌죄), so if the victim does not want punishment, no indictment can be filed. Because it is not an offense prosecutable only on complaint (친고죄), the six-month period for filing a complaint does not apply either. If there is a lot of room for dispute, it may be better to argue public interest and identifiability first in a written opinion rather than rushing into a settlement.

If, on the other hand, you are the victim, the order of steps matters. You can explain the infringement to the board operator and request deletion or a temporary measure, and the temporary measure lasts up to 30 days (Article 44-2 of the Network Act). But you need to capture the original post, its address and the date and time it was written before it disappears, so that evidence remains when you later file a complaint.

author: kim-hansol

title: The investigator's first call: you do not need to explain at length
summary: Many people tell the whole story of their case in the first call from the police. We have set out what to confirm on that call and what to hold back.

body.text: You answer a call from an unknown number and the caller says they are from a police investigation team. After confirming your name, they tell you that you need to come in for questioning about a certain matter. When we hear about this first call in consultations, quite a few people say that, in their shock, they explained their situation at length right then and there. Some even say they spent more than ten minutes justifying themselves, starting with “No, it's not like that.”

It is natural to feel wronged first. But that call is not an interview, and nothing ensures your explanation will be recorded the way you meant it. Investigators sometimes write up the content of the call in an investigation report.
What to write down on this call

Your task on the first call is to confirm, not to explain. Pick up a pen and ask about and note down the following. If the unfamiliar number seems suspicious, it is safer to hang up and call the main number of that police station to ask for the officer in charge.

items: Which police station and team the caller belongs to, and their name
The case number, the charge, and who filed the complaint
Whether you are being called as a suspect or as a witness
Possible dates for appearing and any documents you are asked to bring

body.text: If you are being called as a suspect, the summons must state the gist of the alleged facts (Article 19(3) of the Investigation Rules (수사준칙)). If you were contacted only by phone because the matter is said to be urgent, you may ask them to send you a text message stating what facts you are being questioned about.

Hearing that you are a witness is no reason to relax yet. Questioning that begins with you as a witness sometimes turns into questioning as a suspect depending on what you say. Once you have confirmed in what capacity you are being called, you can decide how much preparation it needs.
You do not have to fix a date now

The investigator may ask you to set a date on the spot. If you need time to prepare, you can say you will check your schedule and call back. Investigators must agree the date, time and place of questioning with the suspect, and if you ask for a postponement they are to adjust it unless there are special circumstances (Article 19(1)3 and 19(2) of the Investigation Rules).

Avoiding contact, or failing to show up on the agreed day without a word, is a different matter. If you do not comply with a summons without a justifiable reason, an arrest warrant may be requested (Article 200-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Even if you postpone the date, do not cut off contact.
When you still want to say something

Sometimes the investigator asks about the facts, saying, ‘I'll just ask you a few simple things.’ In that case it is enough to reply politely that you will give the details when you come in. You need not worry about seeming rude. A calm explanation given in the interview room with your materials in order is a far more useful statement for the investigator as well.

After you hang up, write down what you remember of the call just as it was. As a party to the conversation, recording the call is not a problem either, but more useful than a recording is a note written right after hanging up. What the investigator asked can be a clue to the direction of the investigation. Once you appoint defense counsel, further scheduling is arranged with your lawyer.

author: kim-hansol

title: The right to remain silent is used question by question
summary: When people hear ‘the right to remain silent’, they tend to picture someone refusing to answer every question. We explain the right to refuse to make statements, which can be used question by question, and how to decide when to use it.

body.text: In TV dramas, remaining silent usually means saying nothing at all to the very end. Perhaps that is why people feel that using the right to refuse to make statements means confronting the investigator, or they walk into the interview room without even thinking of it. In actual questioning, the right is used far more precisely than that.
The law has spoken of ‘individual questions’ from the start

Before questioning, the investigator must inform you that you may refuse to make any statement or decline to answer individual questions, that you will suffer no disadvantage for not making a statement, and that what you say may be used as evidence of guilt in court (Article 244-3(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act). It is not all or nothing; you can choose question by question.

After informing you of this, the investigator must ask whether you will exercise the right to refuse to make statements (진술거부권) and the right to the assistance of counsel, and record your answer in the interrogation record (paragraph (2) of the same Article). This exchange on the first page of the record looks like a formality, but it is the record showing whether you were properly informed of your rights.

So it is possible to explain your personal details and how the events unfolded while declining to answer only certain points. Conversely, you can also refuse to answer most questions and state only the facts that are truly necessary. Which approach is better differs from case to case.
Which questions to stop at

In consultations, the situations where we consider refusing to answer are usually these: questions asking you to pin down specific dates or amounts when you have no idea what material the investigators hold, questions about the roles of others involved, and questions asking you to answer even by guessing when your memory is vague. A hasty answer to such questions looks like a changed story later when it conflicts with objective evidence.

When you decline, it is enough to say briefly, ‘I will not answer that part now.’ There is no need to explain your reasons at length or argue with the investigator. For the points where you held back, the option remains to explain them in a written opinion after checking the record and gathering materials.

Things are different in a case where you admit the charge and ask for leniency. Admitting your wrongdoing and explaining honestly how it happened is itself something that is considered in the disposition and sentencing, so refusing to answer often does not help.
Silence is recorded too

If you refuse to answer, the record states exactly that you declined to make a statement. That you will suffer no disadvantage is the law's promise, but in a case with enough other evidence, silence alone will not change the outcome. The right is better used not as a way to cover up a case but as a way to avoid leaving unprepared answers in the record.

Having refused once does not mean you can never speak afterwards. You may give a statement at the next questioning after checking the record. But an explanation given then is only convincing if it is supported by materials that existed from the beginning.
Which questions to stop at should be decided before questioning. If you choose on the spot in the interview room, speech and silence get mixed together and the record ends up looking awkward instead.

author: kim-hansol

title: The night you get a call saying a family member has been arrested
summary: When you hear about an arrest, your first impulse is to rush to the police station. We set out what the family should do first that night, and the difference between a family visit and a meeting with defense counsel.

body.text: News of an arrest usually comes without warning, and often at night or on a weekend. It may be a call from the police made on the person's own mobile phone, or a notice of arrest sent by the police station. After hanging up, most people grab their coat and head for the station, because they feel they will only be at ease once they have seen their family member's face.
A family visit and a meeting with counsel are different

Even if you go to the station, questioning often continues right after the arrest, so families frequently come home without seeing the person. Even if you do meet, it is just a brief chance to ask how they are, and since the conversation may be overheard or recorded, it is hard to talk about the case.

Defense counsel, or a person seeking to become defense counsel, may meet the arrested person (Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act). This meeting is where you can discuss what happened, what has been said in questioning so far, and how to give statements from here on. The spouse, lineal relatives and siblings of the arrested person may appoint defense counsel independently of the person (Article 30(2)). Since the arrested person cannot use a mobile phone, in practice the family has to act first.

If the arrested person has no defense counsel, the police must, within 24 hours of the arrest, notify a family member or other person designated by the arrested person in writing of the name of the case, the date, time and place of arrest, the gist of the alleged offense and the reason for arrest (Article 33(1) of the Investigation Rules (수사준칙)). If you receive this notice, take a photo of it, because its contents are the first information defense counsel will check.
The number 48 hours

If a detention warrant is not requested within 48 hours of the arrest, the person must be released (Article 200-2(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act). Questioning continues during this time, and those statements become material for the warrant application and the pre-detention hearing (영장실질심사). An arrested person in a state of panic tends to answer whatever they are asked. The quickest help a family can give is to have defense counsel meet them before the next round of questioning.

Meanwhile, the family gathers documents for the pre-detention hearing: documents showing that this person is not someone who will flee or destroy evidence, such as a resident registration certificate, a family relations certificate and a certificate of employment. Also write down on paper the time of arrest, the police station, the department in charge and the charge.

The time of arrest is the starting point for counting the 48 hours. If the arrested person is taking any medication, it is also the family's job to bring the name of the medicine and the prescription and inform the police station.
What not to do that night

items: Contacting the victim or others involved in the case to explain the situation
Clearing out the arrested person's mobile phone or computer
Guessing what the arrested person might have said and getting your stories straight with other family members or acquaintances

body.text: If something you did in haste is read as an attempt to sway witnesses or destroy evidence, it can instead hasten the very detention you were trying to prevent. What the family needs to do that night is simpler than you might think: write things down, gather documents, and hand them to defense counsel.
Arrests happen at any hour. Jisan Law takes requests for meetings at night and on weekends as well.

author: kim-hansol

title: Detention periods are shorter than you think
summary: Once someone is detained, time seems to stand still, but for investigators and defense counsel the clock runs fast. We set out what to do, and when, within the detention period during the investigation stage.

body.text: When a warrant is issued, the family feels that a long fight has begun. For the person inside, a single day feels as long as a week. Yet the detention period during the investigation stage is kept short by law. That shortness puts pressure on both the investigators and the suspect's side.
Ten days with the police, ten days with the prosecutor

The police must release a suspect if they do not hand the suspect over to the prosecutor within ten days of detention (Article 202 of the Criminal Procedure Act), and the prosecutor must release the suspect if no indictment is filed within ten days of receiving the case (Article 203). If a request for supplementary investigation or the like is needed, the period may be extended once, by no more than ten days, with a judge's permission (Article 205).

The time the documents were at the court for the pre-detention hearing (영장실질심사) and the period of a review of the legality of detention (구속적부심사) are not counted in this detention period (Article 201-2(7) and Article 214-2(13)). So the date counted on a calendar and the actual expiry date can be several days apart. When we take on a detention case, we calculate this expiry date at the first meeting.
What the shortness means

Investigators pack their questioning into this period. The detained person is called out several times at short intervals and asked the same questions while exhausted. Work that would be spread over several months in a case without detention is compressed into just over ten days.

Defense counsel can also be present during questioning while in detention. The most important work in this period is to realign the direction of statements through meetings between sessions and to check points where earlier answers wavered. The more sessions there are, the easier it is for inconsistencies with earlier statements to arise, so at each meeting we go back over what was asked and how it was answered. The person inside does not know what is happening outside, so it is also defense counsel's job to pass on, at meetings, the materials the family has gathered and the progress of settlement talks.
Written opinions and settlements are timed to the clock too

A settlement agreement submitted before the decision on whether to indict is used differently from one submitted after. The former is taken into account in deciding whether to indict, and the latter in deciding the sentence at trial. This is why settlements are pursued urgently in detention cases.

If new circumstances have arisen since the warrant was issued, such as a settlement or restoration of the victim's losses, a review of the legality of detention is also considered within this period. After indictment the route is bail instead, so which procedure to use also depends on the date.
The clock changes after indictment

After indictment, the court's detention period applies. It is two months as a base, and if continued detention is necessary it may be renewed for two months at a time at each level of trial (Article 92 of the Criminal Procedure Act). From this point, bail can be requested.

Preparing a detention case ultimately means counting the days backwards. If you work back from the expiry date to decide when to handle questioning, written opinions, settlement and the review of detention, the family will also know what to prepare by when.

author: kim-hansol

title: If you cannot pay a fine, do you go straight to a workhouse?
summary: When people receive a fine notice but have no money to pay it, many immediately picture being sent to a workhouse. We set out the options you can apply for before that, and their deadlines.

body.text: Once a fine becomes final through a summary order (약식명령) or a judgment, a payment notice arrives some time later. Quite a few people sigh as soon as they see the amount. Money is already tight for living expenses, and now they are told to pay several million won at once; some even say they would rather serve it off in a workhouse.

Before deciding that, there are things you should know. The period for requesting a formal trial in objection to a summary order is seven days from the day you received notice of it (Article 453(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act), and this article concerns what happens after that period has passed and the fine has become final.
How confinement in a workhouse is decided

A fine must be paid within 30 days from the day the judgment becomes final (Article 69(1) of the Criminal Act). If it is not paid, you are confined in a workhouse (노역장 유치) for a period of one day to three years (paragraph (2) of the same Article), and the number of days it converts into is set when the fine is imposed (Article 70(1)). This is the sentence in the judgment or summary order stating how much one day is worth. If you have paid even part of the fine, the days of confinement are reduced in proportion to the amount paid (Article 71 of the Criminal Act).

If you simply leave the notice alone, procedures to enforce the sentence go ahead, and a sentence execution warrant may be issued and you may be taken into custody (Articles 473 and 492 of the Criminal Procedure Act). This is why some people end up being taken to a workhouse straight from a routine police check. You would suddenly be out of contact with your work and family, so if you cannot pay, you should actually act first.
You can pay in installments or defer payment

If you are in financial difficulty, you can apply to the enforcement department of the Public Prosecution Office (공소청) for installment payment or deferral of payment. The basis for this is Article 12 of the Rules on the Enforcement of Property Penalties by the Public Prosecution Office. Eligible people include recipients of basic livelihood benefits, some near-poverty households, persons with disabilities, recipients of unemployment benefits, people who have received a decision to commence individual rehabilitation, and people who themselves, or whose household members, need medical treatment for a month or more, and the prosecutor grants permission after considering your circumstances and ability to pay.

If permission is granted, you are given a deadline of up to six months, which can be extended up to twice, by three months each time, if the grounds remain. If you fail to pay twice without a justifiable reason, the permission may be revoked, so keep to the agreed schedule. When applying, submit documents showing your circumstances, such as a certificate of benefit receipt or a medical certificate.
For fines of 5 million won or less, community service is also possible

If a fine of 5 million won or less has become final and you cannot pay it, you can apply to have it converted to community service instead of the workhouse (Article 4(1) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Execution of Community Service by Persons Who Fail to Pay Fines, and Article 2 of its Enforcement Decree). You apply to a prosecutor at the district public prosecution office with jurisdiction over your place of residence within 30 days of the prosecutor's payment order, and if you have received permission for installment payment or deferral, you can also apply within that deadline.

There are cases in which you cannot apply, such as when you were sentenced to both imprisonment and a fine, so check in advance. Whichever route you choose, the one thing to avoid is putting the notice in a drawer and letting the deadline pass.

author: kim-hansol

title: A suspended indictment does not mean ‘it never happened’
summary: When you receive a suspended indictment, it is easy to think the case is completely over. We set out what a suspended indictment leaves behind and what it means for your life afterwards.

body.text: ‘I received a suspended indictment. So I don't have a criminal record now, right?’ This is a question we often hear on the day the notice of the decision arrives.
It is half right and half wrong. Since you were not tried, you do not have a record of being sentenced. But the case does not become something that never happened.
It is a decision in which the charge is accepted

A suspended indictment (기소유예) is not a finding that there is no charge. It is a decision that, although the crime is recognized, the case will not be sent to trial this time in light of circumstances such as age and environment and what happened after the offense. Even among decisions not to indict, it differs in nature from ‘no charge’ (혐의없음) or ‘not a crime’ (죄가안됨).

It is a decision often made where a settlement has been reached with the victim, or where it is a first offense and the harm is not serious. In cases where the charge is admitted, it is also often the outcome that defense counsel's written opinion aims for.

So for someone who disputed the charge to the end, a suspended indictment may not be an entirely welcome outcome. There is a way to challenge a suspended indictment received unjustly, but it is narrow and has a fixed deadline, so if you intend to challenge it, you need to seek advice right after receiving the notice. Whether to accept or challenge it is decided by looking at the reasons for the decision together with the record so far.
The record remains for a certain period

Records of having been investigated are kept as investigation history data. A suspended indictment received as an adult is kept for five or ten years from the date of the decision, depending on the statutory penalty for the offense (Article 8-2(2) of the Act on the Lapse of Criminal Sentences). If you were a juvenile at the time of the decision, it is three years (paragraph (3) of the same Article).

This data is kept separately from criminal history data, what is commonly called a criminal record. Even so, if you are investigated again for the same kind of conduct, investigators will check the earlier suspended indictment. The fact that a person who was once shown leniency repeated the same wrongdoing weighs heavily in the second decision. The first suspended indictment, in effect, becomes an unfavorable factor in the second case.

Overseas visa applications and some hiring processes ask about criminal records or investigation history. What must be disclosed, and to what extent, depends on the standards of that country or organization, so it is safer to check separately before submitting documents.
Homework left after the decision

Sometimes a suspended indictment comes with conditions, such as completing education or taking part in a counseling program. If you received such conditions, finish them within the deadline you were given. If money you agreed to pay in installments as part of a settlement is still outstanding, keep that promise to the end as well. If you break it and the victim raises the matter again, things get complicated.

Depending on your occupation, such as public servants or certain licensed professions, even a suspended indictment can be linked to disciplinary action or licensing issues. If this applies to you, it is a good idea to check separately whether you must report it to your organization after receiving the decision, and what procedures follow.
A suspended indictment means you have been given another chance. You may put the decision deep in a drawer, but the years after it will show how you used that chance.

author: kim-hansol

title: Settlement: when should you raise it?
summary: Before the amount of a settlement, what you need to think about is when to start talking about one. We set out what a settlement means at each stage and the problems that arise when you rush.

body.text: ‘When is the right time to settle?’ The answer lies somewhere between ‘the sooner the better’ and ‘don't rush.’ Both are true, which makes it all the more confusing. In criminal settlements, even the same amount of money can lead to different results depending on when and how you raise it.
A settlement does different work at each stage

For offenses that cannot be punished if the victim does not want punishment, such as assault or intimidation, the case can end on the spot once the victim's wish not to have the offender punished (처벌불원) is submitted. This wish must be expressed before the first-instance judgment is pronounced, and once expressed it cannot be withdrawn (Article 232(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act). For offenses that can be punished even after a settlement, such as fraud, embezzlement or bodily injury, where the settlement is taken into account differs by stage.

items: Police stage: it is taken into account in whether the case is referred to the prosecutor and in the prosecutor's later judgment
Before indictment: it is a major factor in deciding whether to end the case with a suspended indictment or a summary order
During trial: it is taken into account in sentencing, and continues to matter until the sentence is pronounced
